alt_description: Killing a brahmin, drinking liquor, theft (of gold), violating the teacher's bed, and association with these; for all of them the name of Viṣṇu is the best expiation (BhP 6.2.9-10).

name: Lack of great faith
description: Doubt that the Lord will protect undermines surrender; great faith (mahāviśvāsa) is its most essential limb.

name: The three defects of the mind: impurity, distraction, veiling
description: Impurity (mala) removed by selfless action, distraction (vikṣepa) removed by meditation/worship (upāsanā), and veiling (āvaraṇa) removed by knowledge — the rationale of the ordered sections of the Veda and Gītā.

name: The intercalary month as unfit for rites
description: The intercalary (adhika) or 'impure' month, in which sacraments, marriages, consecrations and many optional rites are not performed (Kālamādhava; Nirṇayasindhu).

name: Impurities in the channels
description: Channels clogged with impurities prevent the breath from entering the central channel, so unmanī cannot arise (HYP 2.4; GS 5.35).

name: Defiled mind (malina-cetas)
description: In a defiled mind the seed of instruction does not sprout; not even a reflection appears, as in a soiled mirror (SS 4.29–30).

name: Impure latent tendencies (malina vāsanā)
description: Dark, object-bound tendencies that bind to rebirth; to be replaced by pure tendencies such as friendliness and then abandoned.

name: Mine-ness and I-ness
description: Taking what is not the self as self and what is not one's own as 'mine' - the seed of the tree of saṃsāra; 'mine' is the root of suffering.
antidotes: the axe of knowledge sharpened on good company (MkP 38.12)

name: The sense of 'mine' (mamatva)
description: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Its absence (nirmama) marks the one who attains peace (2.71); Arjuna is to fight free of it (3.30).
notes: The text names only its absence (nirmama); the abstract noun is supplied for the obstacle.

name: The unruly mind
description: The restless mind that wanders while the lips recite, runs after the senses like an elephant or thief, and makes defeat and victory; in Sant Mat the agent of Kāl.

name: Conceit (māna)
description: Conceit 'I am', 'I am better, equal, worse' — the eighth fetter; lingering in the non-returner like the smell of soap in cloth (SN 22.89); uprooted by the perception of impermanence (MN 62).

name: Pride of birth and status (māna)
description: Pride in being a brahmin and in the honour due to householders, and pride based on wealth, kin, fame, deeds and learning; removed by dishonour.

name: Restlessness of mind
description: The wandering mind, the monkey of saṃsāra's forest, to be brought back patiently like a horse in training.

name: The mental doṣas rajas and tamas
description: Rajas and tamas corrupt the mind as the three doṣas corrupt the body; they bind the person to rebirth; they are allayed by knowledge, understanding, steadiness, memory and concentration (Ca Sū 1.57-58; Śā 1.36, 4.34).

name: The diseases of the mind (Rāmcaritmānas)
description: Delusion (moha) is the root; lust is wind, greed phlegm, anger bile; jealousy, pride, hypocrisy and the rest follow; cured only when Rāma's grace brings the true guru as physician, faith, restraint and devotion.

equivalents.note: overlapping list of passions, here cast as bodily humours with delusion at the root

name: Five faults of the body (Maṇḍalabrāhmaṇa)
description: Desire, anger, disturbed breathing, fear and sleep; removed by freedom from willing, forbearance, light food, vigilance and devotion to truth (Maṇḍalabrāhmaṇa 1.2).

name: The defects of mantras (mantra-doṣa)
description: Forty-nine defects that make a mantra fail to protect the practitioner — cut, obstructed, powerless, turned away, deaf, blind, nailed, paralysed, burnt, frightened, asleep, drunk, fainted, robbed of potency, child, youth, old, seedless and the rest (ŚT 2.64–70).

name: Māra
description: The Evil One, who tempts and threatens practitioners and finds his opening in those who roam outside their own pasture (SN 47.6; SN 4; SN 5).

name: Māra's deeds against the perfection of wisdom
description: Slowness or scattering of eloquence, yawning and laughing while copying, weariness, turning to lesser sūtras, false visions of the Buddha denying the teaching.

name: Envy (matsara)
description: Bhagavad Gītā 4.22: the one free of envy (vimatsara), content with what comes unsought and beyond the opposites, is not bound though acting.

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

name: 'I and mine' as māyā
description: The sense of 'I' and 'mine', 'you' and 'yours' is the māyā that holds all beings (Rāma to Lakṣmaṇa).

name: Māyā the swindler
description: Māyā, the great swindler with the noose of the three qualities, who appears in every house in a different form — wealth, the goddess, the idol, the pilgrim-water — and binds all creatures.

name: Māyā
description: Śiva's concealing power by which difference is imagined; personified in the Prabhuliṅgalīle as Māyā sent to seduce Allama; Allama locates it in the mind's desire, not in gold, woman or land.

name: Māyīya mala (the impurity of difference)
description: The appearance of the knowable as separate, which gives birth and experience (ĪPK 3.2.5).
alt_description: The bond of māyā's products — body, organs, worlds — which also help the soul by partly awakening it.

name: Mere non-thought mistaken for wisdom
description: Cultivating the mere absence of recollection and attention without correct analysis; like fainting, it only cultivates delusion and cannot remove the obscurations.

name: Hypocritical restraint (mithyācāra)
description: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: One who restrains the organs of action but sits dwelling in mind on sense-objects is called a hypocrite (3.6); contrasted with one who controls the senses by the mind and undertakes karma-yoga unattached (3.7).
antidotes: Control the senses by the mind and act unattached (3.7)

name: False knowledge (mithyājñāna)
description: The first impurity; removed by the living with the teacher and learning (vāsa).

name: False knowledge (mithyājñāna)
description: The root of the series leading to birth and pain: taking the non-self as self, denying the self, taking pain as pleasure, the impermanent as permanent, the unprotecting as protection, the fearful as safe, the loathsome as desirable; denying karma, its fruit and rebirth; fearing liberation.

equivalents.note: Yoga's avidyā (YS 2.5) has an overlapping list of misapprehensions.

name: Wrong view (mithyātva)
description: Belief contrary to the realities, the first and root cause of bondage; five kinds (one-sided, contrary, indiscriminate reverence, doubt, ignorance — Digambara list) or innate and acquired.
antidotes: right view through the three processes and the breaking of the knot
alt_description: Wrong faith, of five kinds: one-sided, perverse, doubting, vainayika and ajñānika; or, as taught by others, the four vāda classes (363 views).
notes: U33 contribution; U35 owns the Jain account.

name: Delusion (moha)
description: Delusion, born of anger (BhG 2.63) and of the pairs of opposites (7.27), by which the world does not know the Lord (7.13); destroyed by knowledge and grace (4.35; 18.73).
antidotes: Knowledge of the imperishable embodied one (2.13, 2.30)
The brāhmī sthiti, after which one is not deluded (2.72)
the end of sin, freedom from the pairs (7.28)

Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

notes: U05's contribution to a shared obstacle.
alt_description: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Arjuna's mind is bewildered about dharma (2.7); understanding must cross the thicket of delusion (2.52); delusion arises from anger and confuses memory (2.63); those deluded by the guṇas are attached to their actions (3.29); those who cavil are deluded in all knowledge (3.32); desire deludes the embodied one through the senses, mind and understanding (3.40). The one in the brahmic state is not bewildered (2.72).

Bhagavad Gītā 7–9: the whole world, deluded by the three guṇa-made states, does not recognize the Lord (7.13); the deluded (mūḍha) evil-doers do not take refuge in him (7.15); the deluded world does not know him, veiled by yoga-māyā (7.25); all beings fall into bewilderment at birth through the delusion of the pairs (7.27); the deluded disregard him in human form (9.11) and resort to a deluding nature (9.12).
The third unwholesome root, one of the three fires.

Knowledge taught by the truth-seers frees one from falling into delusion again (4.35); creatures are deluded because knowledge is covered by ignorance (5.15); the knower of Brahman is undeluded (5.20).
Delusion veils the yogin so that only powers, not liberation, result (Śiva Sūtra 3.6); one struck down by delusion is bound by karma (3.35).

name: Delusion (moha)
description: The worst fault, since attachment and aversion arise only in the deluded.

name: The thirty grounds of deluding karma
description: Acts so grave that they bind the strongest deluding karma — killing beings cruelly, betraying a teacher or the community, falsely claiming to be a monk or omniscient, and others — listed in the ninth chapter of the Daśāśrutaskandha.

name: The fetters of death (mṛtyu-pāśa)
description: Death's fetters, from which the long-life rites lift a person 'with divine speech'; the Tryambaka verse asks release from death, not from immortality.
notes: rests_on: tea:atharvaveda-saunaka:8.1.1-10, tea:rgveda:7.59.12

name: Attachment (mūrcchā)
description: Infatuation with what one has — the inner essence of possessiveness ('possession is attachment'); one who gives up the thought 'mine' gives up what is his.

name: The ten offences against the name
description: Blaspheming devotees; regarding Śiva's names and qualities as independent of Viṣṇu's; disregarding the guru; deriding scripture; taking the name's glories as exaggeration; interpreting the name fancifully; sinning on its strength; equating it with other pious acts; teaching it to the faithless; lacking love for it despite hearing its glories (clinging to 'I and mine'); inattention is often added.
members: no love despite hearing its glory
alt_description: Reviling devotees, separating Śiva's names from Viṣṇu's, disregarding the teacher, deriding scripture, calling the name's glory exaggeration, interpreting it away, sinning on its strength, equating it with other pious acts, teaching it to the faithless, and indifference despite hearing its glory (as cited from the Padma).
Ekaśaraṇa: the Kīrtana-ghoṣā's section on offences against the name (list to verify), which constant singing of the name itself removes.

name: Unbelief (nāstikya) and the 'Lokāyata' reading of Mīmāṃsā
description: Denial of the self, the afterlife and the Veda's authority; Kumārila writes to lead Mīmāṃsā, 'mostly made Lokāyata', back onto the āstika path, and presents Śabara's proof of the self as its refutation.

name: The near and far enemies of the divine abidings
description: Each divine abiding is threatened by a near enemy resembling it and a far enemy opposed to it.
members: upekkhā: unknowing equanimity (near), greed and resentment (far)

name: Nidāna (binding wish for reward)
description: Wishing that one's austerities bring worldly or heavenly reward — a thorn, a sorrowful meditation and a fault of the final fast (TS 7.37, 9.33).

name: Being without a guru (nigurā)
description: The one without a guru goes away thirsty from the well of nectar (Gorakh Bānī).

name: Misreading emptiness as nothingness
description: Taking emptiness to mean that nothing exists, so that karma, the path and the Buddha are denied; wrongly seen emptiness destroys the slow-witted like a snake wrongly grasped.

name: The nine obstacles (antarāya), distractions of mind
description: Illness, dullness, doubt, carelessness, laziness, non-abstention, erroneous vision, failure to gain a stage and instability — distractions of the mind, called impurities, adversaries and obstacles of yoga (1.30, YBh 1.30).

name: The nine quasi-passions (nokaṣāya)
description: Laughter, liking, disliking, grief, fear, disgust and the three sexual drives, which accompany the passions (TS 8.9).

name: The nine fetters (Abhidharma list)
description: Attachment, aversion, pride, ignorance, view, clinging, doubt, envy and avarice.

equivalents.note: The Abhidharma nine fetters and the Pali Abhidhamma ten share envy, avarice, pride, views, doubt, ignorance; the lists are divided differently.

alt_description: Yogācāra contribution: the Madhyāntavibhāga (2.1–3) names the nine fetters as the characteristic of affliction — attraction, aversion, pride, ignorance, views, holding to the supreme, doubt, envy and avarice.

name: The ninety-eight latent defilements (anuśaya)
description: The root of existence: six anuśayas (passion, aversion, pride, ignorance, view, doubt), seven with passion split into sensual and existence-passion, ten with the five views; distributed by realm and by what abandons them — the seeing of each truth, or cultivation — they number ninety-eight.

equivalents.note: The seven are the base of the Kośa's ninety-eight, which are counted by realm and mode of abandonment.

name: Nirṛti (dissolution, misfortune)
description: The power of destruction and misfortune, whose lap and fetters threaten the living and the dead.
notes: rests_on: tea:rgveda:10.18.10-13, tea:atharvaveda-saunaka:8.1.1-10

name: Clinging to rules (niyamagraha)
description: Rigid adherence to (unsuitable) observances such as early-morning bathing or fasting (HYP 1.15; Gorakṣa's saying 1.61).

name: The fixed wrong views (niyata-micchādiṭṭhi)
description: The Theravāda commentaries' name for the three views of DN 2 and MN 60 — there is nothing (natthika), no cause (ahetuka), no effect of action (akiriya) — held firmly, which block the path and heaven alike.
notes: The commentarial term is recalled, not checked; the three views themselves are canonical.

name: Offences against women
description: Insulting, mocking, striking or deceiving women angers the Kula yoginīs and blocks perfection (Kulārṇava 11.61-65; Kaulāvalīnirṇaya 10.87-88).

name: Diminution and disorders of ojas
description: Ojas is diminished by injury, wasting, anger, grief, worry, fatigue and hunger; its disorders are displacement, vitiation and loss; in loss one is fearful, weak, anxious, dull, dejected and emaciated, and complete loss is death.
antidotes: avoiding the causes of mental suffering; calm and knowledge (Ca Sū 30.13-14)

name: Outward ritual without inner knowledge
description: Stone images, temple rounds, holy baths, pilgrimage and recitation taken as ends: the Siddhars' main target (Sivavākkiyar; Kaṭuveḷi 15; Pattirakiriyār 16).

name: The householder's five slaughter-places
description: Hearth, grindstone, broom, mortar and pestle, and water-pot, by whose daily use small beings are killed and the householder bound (MDh 3.68).

name: The pañcaka asterisms
description: The five asterisms from the latter half of Dhaniṣṭhā to Revatī, during which certain works and cremation without special rites are avoided.

name: Five-jointed ignorance (Vallabha)
description: Forgetting one's nature and identifying with body, senses, vital breath and inner organ.

name: The five kinds of faults removed by brahmasambandha
description: Innate faults, those arising from place and time, those determined by worldly and Vedic rule, those arising from association and those from contact.

name: Proliferation (papañca)
description: The proliferating perceptions and notions that beset a person after feeling, perception and thought (MN 18), rooted in 'I am' (Snp 4.14), the source of quarrels (Snp 4.11).

name: Evil (pāpman)
description: Evil pierced the senses in the gods' contest, so that one speaks, sees and thinks what is improper (BAU 1.3; ChU 1.2); evils turn back from the self, the dam (ChU 8.4); the knower's evils burn like a reed tuft (ChU 5.24.3), do not cling like water on a lotus leaf (ChU 4.14.3); the self is free from evil (ChU 8.1.5).

name: Knowledge without lineage (pride of book-learning)
description: Knowledge gained from books without the succession of teachers breeds pride and harm (YH 2.81); the flow of the mind to the meaning comes only by the guru's grace (Setubandha).

name: Speaking ill of others
description: Slander and fault-finding, which the true Vaiṣṇava avoids and the saint does not see even in dreams.

name: Possessiveness (parigraha)
description: Grasping at possessions and hoarding, which brings suffering and attack (the osprey, the bee, the honey-gatherer).
alt_description: Holding possessions, living or lifeless — the bond the Sūtrakṛtāṅga names first; defined in both traditions as attachment (mūrcchā), though the Digambaras hold any clothing to show it and the Śvetāmbaras do not.

name: Falling back (parihāṇi)
description: Loss of an attained state: for the Sarvāstivāda possible for five of the six kinds of arhat (not from stream-entry), in three forms; the Sautrāntika denies falling back from arhatship.
antidotes: perfection of the faculties (to the unshakeable lineage)

name: The envelopments (paryavasthāna)
description: Eight (or ten) secondary defilements: shamelessness, lack of dread of blame, envy, avarice, restlessness, remorse, torpor, sleepiness (+ anger, concealment); for the Sautrāntika, 'envelopment' is the awakened defilement.

name: The five Pāśupata impurities (mala)
description: False knowledge, demerit, the cause of attachment, falling away, and the root of the paśu-state - to be abandoned; Kauṇḍinya's list: ignorance, demerit, habituation to objects, non-attainment of steadiness, lack of lordship.

name: The paśu-state (paśutva)
description: Bondage as beginningless lack of lordship; its final removal comes through connection with Maheśvara's lordship.

equivalents.note: both name the soul's root bondage; the Siddhānta's āṇava is an innate impurity, the Pāśupata paśutva lack of lordship

alt_description: Kaula usage: the one bound by the eight fetters is a paśu (Kulārṇava 13.91).

name: Aversion (fetter)
description: The fifth fetter (ill will), abandoned by the non-returner.

name: Attachment and aversion (pejja-dosa, rāga-dveṣa)
description: The two roots of karma under which the four passions are gathered (deceit and greed as attachment, anger and pride as aversion); 'attachment and aversion are the seeds of karma'.

name: Desire for women (peṇṇācai)
description: In the renouncer-poets' own terms, desire for women is the snare that binds to birth; the seeker longs to think of woman as mother (Pattirakiriyār 8, 9–11) and Paṭṭiṉattār laments the women who bewitch. Recorded faithfully as the texts' view.

name: The sea of births and sorrow (piṟavi, iṭar āḻi)
description: The round of births, pictured as an ocean of sorrow, from which the Āḻvārs ask release at the Lord's feet; the false knowledge, evil conduct and impure body in which the soul has stood (Tiruviruttam 1).

name: Affliction from the ancestors (pitṛ-doṣa)
description: The ancestors' displeasure shown in the chart or query, bringing childlessness and repeated misfortune.

name: Aggravation of pitta
description: Pitta increases by anger, grief, fear, fasting, pungent, sour, salty, sharp and hot foods, especially in hot seasons, at midday and midnight and during digestion; increased, it brings yellowness, heat, desire for cold, little sleep, fainting and weakness of the senses.

name: Book-learning without love
description: Reading books till death without becoming wise; speaking of what is written on paper instead of what is seen; for Bāuls, reliance on scripture (anumān).

name: Practice learned from texts without a guru
description: The haṭha texts hold that the techniques succeed only when received from a guru: knowledge from the guru's mouth is potent, otherwise it is fruitless, powerless and brings great suffering (ŚS 3.11); the inverting technique is known from the guru's instruction, not from millions of treatises (HYP 3.78); khecarī requires the guru's mantra (Khecarīvidyā).
antidotes: receiving instruction from a qualified guru and serving him (ŚS 3.12-15)

name: Too much talk (prajalpa)
description: Excessive talking (HYP 1.15; 'much talk' SS 3.33).

name: Failure of discernment (prajñāparādha)
description: The unwholesome act done when intellect, resolve and memory lapse: the provoker of all doṣas, source of mental and exogenous disease, insanity and epidemics (Ca Śā 1.98-109; Sū 7.51-52; Ni 7.10; Vi 3.20).
antidotes: abandoning prajñāparādha, calming the senses, memory, knowledge of place, time and self, good conduct (Ca Sū 7.53)

name: The covering of the light (prakāśāvaraṇa)
description: The karma that covers discriminative knowledge, yoking luminous sattva to what should not be done; it dwindles through prāṇāyāma (2.52, YBh 2.52) and is destroyed by the great bodiless concentration (3.43).

name: Making the secret public (prākaṭya)
description: Exposure of the secret worship leads to hell (PKS 1.12); the Kaula Upaniṣad forbids telling one's secret except to a disciple; Bhāskararāya calls non-exposure the chief of Kaula conducts.

name: Absorption into prakṛti mistaken for liberation
description: Dispassion without discrimination leads to absorption into prakṛti or its evolutes, taken for liberation ('darkness': thinking 'I am liberated'); one rises again like a diver; the Kramadīpikā calls it bondage to prakṛti.

name: Absorption in prakṛti or the bodiless state short of kaivalya
description: The bodiless and those merged in prakṛti experience a state 'as if' of kaivalya but return when their impressions ripen or the mind's unfinished task draws it back (1.19, YBh 1.19); lower dispassion includes giving up the wish for these states (YBh 1.15).
notes: Framed as an obstacle by this unit on the basis of YBh 1.15 and 1.19; the sūtra itself only states the cause of their state.

name: Heedlessness (pramāda)
description: Heedlessness is death (Sanatsujāta, MBh 5.42.4); negligence is a bond of tamas (BhG 14.8).

alt_description: Not cultivating the means of samādhi; Vyāsa warns that carelessness, ever watching for an opening, revives the afflictions (YBh 3.51). One of the nine obstacles (1.30, YBh 1.30).

Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): 'do not neglect truth, dharma, study' (TU 1.11); the target is to be pierced by one who is undistracted (MuU 2.2.4); not attained through heedlessness (MuU 3.2.4); in yoga one becomes undistracted (KU 2.3.11).
Inattention to what is to come and dependence; the end of suffering is reached by the vigilant.

name: Carelessness (pramāda)
description: Heedlessness in conduct — gossip, passions, indulgence of the senses, sleep, affection — which makes an injury 'violence' (TS 7.13, 8.1).

equivalents.note: YS 1.30 pramāda is neglect of the means to samādhi.

name: Doubt about the means of knowledge (pramāṇa-saṃśaya)
description: Doubt whether the Upaniṣads really teach the non-dual Brahman; removed by hearing.

name: Doubt about the object (prameya-saṃśaya, asambhāvanā)
description: Doubt whether the self can possibly be Brahman; removed by reflection.

name: Conceptual elaboration (prapañca)
description: Verbal-conceptual elaboration from which conceptual construction, action and afflictions arise; those who elaborate the Buddha do not see him.

equivalents.note: Pali papañca in the Madhupiṇḍika Sutta is proliferation rooted in craving, conceit and views

name: Begun karma (prārabdha)
description: Karma that has begun to bear fruit continues until the body falls; for this reason there is no liberation while living. For the distressed surrenderer the Lord ends it at once.
alt_description: Karma that has begun to bear fruit; it continues to be experienced after direct knowledge until the body falls, and new karma is always being made, so karma cannot be exhausted by experience alone.
notes: The prārabdha doctrine is recorded from general Vedānta knowledge; only BSB 3.1.8 was checked.

name: Attachment even to the good (praśasta-rāga)
description: Even affection for the teacher binds: Gautama's love for Mahāvīra delayed his omniscience until the night of Mahāvīra's nirvāṇa, when he cut that bond.
antidotes: reflection on the Jina's own detachment

name: Obstructions to knowledge (pratibandha)
description: Knowledge arises in this life only if no obstruction is present (BS 3.4.51): present obstructions (attachment to objects, dull intellect, perverse reasoning, obstinate misconception), past tendencies, and future karma requiring further births.

name: Desire for prestige (pratiṣṭhāśā)
description: The desire for fame and honour, 'a shameless outcaste woman dancing in the heart', the most persistent anartha, which keeps pure love out.

name: Pratyavāya (demerit of omission)
description: The demerit incurred by failing to perform enjoined obligatory and occasional rites (and, for Śabara, the harm to which rites like the Śyena lead).

name: Other cognitions in the gaps of discernment
description: In the gaps of a mind flowing with discernment, cognitions such as 'I am', 'mine', 'I know', 'I do not know' arise from dwindling impressions (4.27, YBh 4.27); they are removed as the afflictions are (4.28).

name: Overexertion (prayāsa)
description: Excessive exertion (HYP 1.15).

name: Choosing the pleasant over the good
description: The fool chooses the pleasant (preyas) for the sake of getting and keeping; the child deluded by wealth thinks 'this is the world, there is no other' and falls again into Death's power (KU 1.2.2, 1.2.6).
antidotes: discerning the good from the pleasant, as Naciketas did (KU 1.1.21-29)

checks.note: All 4 Upaniṣad refs cited in the entry are located in the prepared segments (KU 1.2.2; KU 1.2.6; KU 1.1.21-29; KU 1.2.1-6). It rests on 2 teaching(s) text-located in this sweep, and its wording matches those passages.

name: Pride and conceit (abhimāna)
description: Claiming attainments not reached (the five thousand who left the Lotus assembly); bodhisattvas' anger and contempt toward one another.

name: The ten obstacles of yoga (Liṅga/Śiva Purāṇa)
description: Sloth, illness, heedlessness, doubt about the ground, unsteadiness of mind, faithlessness, erroneous views, threefold suffering, dejection and restless craving for objects; they perish for one of great zeal.

name: Defects of a (human) speaker
description: Delusion and other defects that make human testimony about what is beyond the senses unreliable; since defects of words depend on speakers, the authorless Veda is free of them.

name: Curses from a former birth
description: Afflictions such as the loss of offspring that the chart shows to arise from sins or curses of a former birth — of serpents, ancestors, mother, brother, brahmins, spirits — each with its expiation (BPHS 83; Praśna Mārga).
notes: Member list recalled from BPHS 83 (from memory beyond the chapter opening).

name: Passion, attachment (rāga)
description: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Passion or attraction (rāga), set together with aversion in each sense towards its object, is a waylayer; one should not come under its sway (3.34). The self-governed person moves among objects with senses free of attraction and aversion and attains serenity (2.64); the sage of steady mind is free from passion, fear and anger (vītarāgabhayakrodha, 2.56).
antidotes: Move among objects with senses free of passion and aversion, under control (2.64)

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

alt_description: Sāṃkhya contribution: from passion of the nature of rajas comes saṃsāra (SK 45); meditation is its removal (SS 3.30); it is not quieted by enjoyment but by seeing the faults (SS 4.27–28); brooding on what is not a means binds, as with Bharata (SS 4.8).
Attachment follows on pleasure (2.7).
Many free of passion, fear and anger, absorbed in the Lord, reached his state (4.10); the constant renouncer does not crave (5.3).

name: Attachment (rāga)
description: Attachment to the agreeable, arising from false knowledge and from the notion of the whole; in Vaiśeṣika it arises from pleasure, absorption, satisfaction, the unseen and particular birth.

name: Demons and sorcerers (rakṣas, yātudhāna)
description: Harmful beings who disturb the rite and cause disease, driven off by Agni, Indra-Soma and the healer.
notes: rests_on: tea:rgveda:10.97.6, tea:rgveda:7.104.15

name: The impurities of mercury
description: Mercury carries natural impurities (poison, fire, dirt) and adventitious 'coverings' — twelve in RRS — each causing disease or death; with them mercury is poison (Rasaratnākara Rasa 1.27-30; RRS 11.20-25). RESTRICTED context.
antidotes: purification by the qualified under a guru (no procedure recorded)

name: Craving of the tongue
description: Greed for taste, the sense that grows stronger with fasting and is conquered last; when taste is conquered all is conquered.

name: The seven obstacles to aesthetic relish (rasa-vighna)
description: Lack of credibility; being caught in the particular time and place of oneself or another; being overwhelmed by one's own pleasure or pain; lack of the means of perception; lack of clarity; non-predominance of the stable emotion; and doubt (Abhinavagupta).
antidotes: the preliminaries, music and conventions of the stage

equivalents.note: in Advaita the relish of bliss is itself an obstacle to samādhi; in poetics the obstacles are what block relish

name: Relishing the bliss (rasāsvāda)
description: Enjoying the bliss of absorption (savikalpa) and resting there, which prevents going beyond; one should be unattached through discernment (GK 3.45).
alt_description: The mind turning to taste worldly pleasures during practice.
notes: Partial parallel: Vedāntasāra's rasāsvāda (there: relishing the bliss of savikalpa samādhi) — same word, different object (list of obstacles to nirvikalpa samādhi; U13). Viśvanātha adds apratipatti.

name: Semblance of devotional emotion (ratyābhāsa)
description: Apparent ecstasy or emotion — reflected or shadow-like — in those whose hearts are impure or whose aims are other; outward signs imitated without bhāva.

name: The six faults of reciters
description: Singing, hurrying, shaking the head, reading from a written text, not knowing the meaning, and a weak voice (PŚ 32).

checks.note: PŚ 32 has 'gītī śīghrī śiraḥkampī tathā likhitapāṭhakaḥ | anarthajño 'lpakaṇṭhaś ca ṣaḍ ete pāṭhakādhamāḥ'; the six members match, within the cited 31–33. This rests on tea:paniniya-siksa:31-33.

name: Rejecting the true dharma (saddharmapratikṣepa)
description: Denying that the Mahāyāna sūtras are the Buddha's word; a karma worse than the five deadly acts, excluded from the eighteenth vow, and the mark of the icchantika.

name: Relying on favourable planets or on rites alone
description: Expecting success from favourable planets, asterisms and times alone, or from mantras, amulets, pacifications and oblations alone, without human effort and the other means: 'the astrologer would be king… the priest would be king' (Yogayātrā 1.5–6).
antidotes: human effort (puruṣakāra) joined with fate, like farming (Yogayātrā 1.3–4)

equivalents.note: both warn against leaning on fate instead of effort; Varāhamihira still requires fate and good timing alongside effort, the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha denies fate any power of its own

name: What binds or makes a renouncer fall
description: A fixed seat, loss of bowl, hoarding, gathering disciples for gain, sleep and idle talk (Sannyāsa 2.79–85); couch, white clothes, talk of women, day-sleep and vehicles (Nāradaparivrājaka 3.69–71).

name: The restless mind
description: The mind is restless, turbulent, strong and obstinate, as hard to restrain as the wind (BhG 6.34); it wanders from the object of meditation (6.26).
antidotes: bringing the mind back into the self wherever it wanders (6.26)

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; corrections logged in interpretation_log.jsonl.

alt_description: Arjuna does not see how the yoga of sameness can stand steady because of restlessness (6.33): the mind is restless, turbulent, strong and obstinate, as hard to restrain as the wind (6.34); Kṛṣṇa agrees it is hard to restrain (6.35); it wanders off (6.26).

name: Revealing what must be hidden
description: Revealing the mantra, or hiding the guru, destroys wealth and life (Kulārṇava 11.88); open worship destroys perfection (Kālīvilāsa 7.11); the Kaula essence is not to be given to the deceitful (Kaulajñānanirṇaya 6.14).

name: Lust for form
description: The sixth fetter: lust for existence in the fine-material realm.

name: The twenty-one grave faults (śabala)
description: Faults that 'spot' a monk's conduct, such as accepting food prepared for him, eating at night, repeated minor violations of vows — listed in the Daśāśrutaskandha.

name: The six enemies (ṣaḍ-ripu)
description: Desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride and envy, the six obstacles to yoga pierced by its limbs (Devī Gītā).

name: Hunger, thirst, sorrow, delusion, old age and death
description: The self within all is beyond hunger and thirst, sorrow and delusion, old age and death (BAU 3.5.1); the self free from evil is without old age, death, sorrow, hunger and thirst (ChU 8.1.5, 8.7.1).
notes: The name 'six waves' (ṣaḍūrmi) is later Vedānta usage (moderate).

checks.note: Members located: BĀU 3.5.1 ('aśanāyāpipāse śokaṃ mohaṃ jarāṃ mṛtyum atyeti'); ChU 8.1.5 and 8.7.1 (vijaro vimṛtyur viśoko vijighatso 'pipāsaḥ). The name ṣaḍūrmi is rightly marked as later usage. All 3 Upaniṣad refs cited in the entry are located in the prepared segments (BĀU 3.5.1; ChU 8.1.5; ChU 8.7.1). It rests on 3 teaching(s) text-located in this sweep, and its wording matches those passages.

name: Saturn's seven and a half years (sāḍhe-sātī)
description: Saturn's transit through the 12th, 1st and 2nd signs from the natal Moon, a time of trials in popular teaching, following the classical rule that Saturn is good only in the 3rd, 6th and 11th from the Moon (BS 103.4).

name: The six enemies: desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, envy
description: Kāma, krodha, lobha, moha, mada, mātsarya - in their grip the Vijñāna Bhairava teaches making the understanding motionless so that reality remains (VBT 101; cf. 96 on quieting a desire at its source).

name: Acting with desire for fruits
description: Action done for its results; desirelessness, flawless service and fitness are the conditions for seeing Hari, and ritual works done for results win only the lowest grace (heaven).

name: Identity view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi)
description: Regarding the aggregates as self in twenty ways (MN 44); the first fetter, abandoned at stream-entry.

name: The cause of attachment (saktihetu)
description: The third impurity, whose removal is the third purification.

name: Intrusion of objects and bodily urges in samādhi
description: Objects intrude by their force, and hunger and the like drive one away, so that samādhi seems impossible; overcome through the continuing effect of previous practice.

name: The imperfections of concentration
description: Doubt, inattention, sloth and torpor, fear, elation, inertia, excess energy, slack energy, longing, perception of diversity and excessive meditation on forms, which make the light and vision of forms vanish (MN 128).

name: Breaking the samaya pledges
description: Without the samaya discipline there is no perfection and one falls from the Kula (Kulārṇava 5.96); disciples who do not honour the samayas become tāmasa (Kubjikāmata 12.3-9).
antidotes: asking the guru's pardon and worshipping the transmission (Kubjikāmata 12.10)
alt_description: Knowingly breaking the rules taken at initiation is a great fault; through ignorance it is no fault.

name: Breach of the samaya
description: Breaking the initiate's observances; for those without lineage and proud of mere knowledge, through this breach the mantra's rays turn against them (YH 2.81).

equivalents.note: the Śrīvidyā statement of the Mantramārga fault of breaking initiatory rules

name: Schism of the Saṅgha (saṅghabheda)
description: Dividing the community by a rival teacher and path (wheel-schism) or by separate legal acts (act-schism); caused by a monk of views; its lie ripens in Avīci for an aeon.

name: Doubt (saṃśaya)
description: The doubting self perishes; for the doubter there is neither this world nor the next nor happiness (BhG 4.40); doubt born of ignorance is to be cut with the sword of knowledge (4.42).
antidotes: the teacher who can cut the doubt (6.39)

alt_description: A cognition touching both alternatives: 'it may be so, it may not'. One of the nine obstacles (1.30, YBh 1.30).

Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): Śāṇḍilya's meditation succeeds for one who has 'no doubt' (ChU 3.14.4); when he is seen all doubts are cut (MuU 2.2.8); free from doubt he becomes a brahmin (BAU 4.4.23); Naciketas's doubt about the dead (KU 1.1.20).
Worship of one guru is to be without doubt (PKS 1.20); all success comes through tradition and faith (PKS 1.9-10).

Bhagavad Gītā 4.40–42: the one of doubting mind (saṃśayātman) perishes and has neither this world nor the next nor happiness; doubt is born of ignorance and lodged in the heart; the seers who attain brahma-nirvāṇa have their doubts cut (5.25); Arjuna asks the Lord to cut his doubt about the fallen yogin (6.39).

name: Enjoyments born of contact (saṃsparśaja bhoga)
description: Bhagavad Gītā 5.21–22: enjoyments born of contact are wombs of suffering and have a beginning and an end; the wise do not delight in them; the one unattached to external contacts finds happiness in the self.

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

antidotes: non-attachment to external contacts and the happiness found in the self (5.21)

name: Transgressions of right view
description: Doubt, desire, disgust, praise of wrong-believers and intimacy with them (TS 7.23).

name: Attachment (saṅga)
description: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Attachment arises from dwelling on objects and gives rise to desire (2.62); it is to be abandoned in action (2.48, 3.9) and is not to be directed to inaction (2.47); those attached to enjoyment and power lack resolute understanding (2.44); the ignorant are attached to action and to the actions of the guṇas (3.26, 3.29).
antidotes: Act unattached, for sacrifice and lokasaṃgraha (3.9, 3.19, 3.25); know that 'the guṇas move among the guṇas' (3.28)

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

alt_description: Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: for the one whose attachment is gone action dissolves (4.23); one acting with actions placed in Brahman and abandoning attachment is unstained (5.10); yogins act abandoning attachment (5.11); one unattached to external contacts finds happiness in the self (5.21); one unattached to sense objects and actions has ascended to yoga (6.4).

name: Attachment (saṅga)
description: Attachment that overturns even an ascetic's practice: Bharata's love for a fawn, Saubhari's longing on seeing mating fish.
antidotes: avoiding the company of the attached
keeping the senses from going outward (BhP 9.6.51)

name: Attachment and pride at the celestials' invitation
description: At the honey stage the gods invite the yogin with pleasures, elixirs, sky-cars and nymphs; attachment would make him fuel for saṃsāra again, and pride ('even the gods desire me') lets carelessness revive the afflictions (3.51, YBh 3.51).
antidotes: reflection on the faults of attachment (YBh 3.51)

name: Doubt and scruple (śaṅkā), especially about purity
description: Doubt and scruples about purity and impurity bind: the purity prescribed by those of little knowledge is impurity in Śambhu's vision (VBT 123); in the Krama phases, the Yama Kālī gives rise to and removes doubt (TĀ 4.151-152).

name: Intention (saṅkalpa) as bondage
description: Intention is absent from the undertakings of the wise (4.19); no one becomes a yogin without renouncing it (6.2); the one ascended to yoga has renounced all intentions (6.4); desires are born of intention (6.24).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

alt_description: The mind's conceiving that spins worlds; its cure ends saṃsāra for oneself.

name: Contraction (saṅkoca)
description: The contraction of universal consciousness into the individual knower, who consists of the universe in contracted form (PH 4, 9).

name: Combined aggravation of all three doṣas (sannipāta)
description: All three doṣas provoked together — the gravest imbalance, often incurable; the stronger doṣa is treated first without opposing the others.

name: Affliction from the serpents (sarpa-doṣa)
description: In the Kerala tradition, affliction traced to harming serpents or neglecting their shrines, shown in the query and remedied by serpent worship.

name: Censure of other schools
description: Censuring any school is forbidden (PKS 1.14; Kaula Upaniṣad): the schools are valid for their own qualified followers, and censure makes them doubt their own way without qualifying them for the Kaula (Bhāskararāya).

name: The view of eternalism (sassata-diṭṭhi)
description: The extreme that self and world are eternal; often grounded in meditative recollection of past lives.

name: The 'śaṭha' wind of forgetting
description: In the hagiographies, the wind (śaṭha-vāyu) that touches every newborn and makes it forget its knowledge; Nammāḻvār repelled it at birth, hence his name Śaṭhakopa ('angry at śaṭha').
notes: Hagiographic teaching, the tradition's account.

name: The view of the transitory collection
description: The view that takes the aggregates as 'I' and 'mine', from which all afflictions and faults arise.

equivalents.note: the same view named in Pali; the first of the fetters

name: Self-cherishing (desiring one's own happiness)
description: All who suffer in the world suffer from desiring their own happiness; all calamities and fears come from grasping at self.

name: Self-grasping as the root of faults
description: Seeing a self produces love for it, thirst for happiness, appropriation of means as 'mine', the division of self and other, clinging and aversion, and all faults; as long as it lasts one is in saṃsāra.

name: The sense of 'I am the doer' (kartṛtva-abhimāna)
description: Deluded by ego one thinks 'I am the doer' of actions done by the guṇas of prakṛti (BhG 3.27); one who sees the self alone as agent does not see (18.16).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

alt_description: The yoked knower of reality thinks 'I do nothing at all', holding that the senses move among their objects (5.8–9); the lord creates neither agency nor actions nor their link with fruit — svabhāva acts (5.14). Chs. 4–6 do not use the compound kartṛtva-abhimāna.

name: Offences in deity worship (sevāparādha)
description: Offences against the deity in worship — impurity, disrespect, improper conduct in the temple — listed in the Haribhaktivilāsa (from the Purāṇas); number and list to verify.

name: The seven latent tendencies (anusaya)
description: Latent tendencies to sensual lust, aversion, conceit, views, doubt, lust for existence and ignorance, lying dormant in specific feelings and spheres.
alt_description: Tendencies to sensual lust, aversion, views, doubt, conceit, lust for becoming and ignorance (MN 18; AN 7.11), latent in feelings (MN 44; MN 148) and even in an infant (MN 64).

name: The seven bonds (Amaraughaśāsana)
description: Desire, anger, greed, delusion, intoxication, pride and egoism bind the embodied one (AmŚ 25); the Kaula text also bids one give up desire, anger, pride and greed little by little (KJN 11.31).

name: The seven unsuitable things
description: Unsuitable dwelling, resort, speech, person, food, climate and posture, which cause the sign to be lost.
antidotes: resorting to the seven suitable things

name: The eight passions (irākam)
description: Among the ninety-six principles: desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, envy, haughtiness and egoism (list recalled at low confidence).

name: Pride in powers
description: Powers (siddhi) and the pride they breed: Cāṅgadev's power over beasts was humbled; māyā sends the powers to blow out the lamp of knowledge; a guru who displays powers is false.

name: Attachment to powers
description: U21 contribution: powers, the nether regions and alchemy, even when obtained, are nets of bondage leading down; they are not to be grasped (Akulavīra B.83–84).
alt_description: The sixty-four tantras, each bent on producing its own particular powers, beguiled the world; the Goddess's tantra alone accomplishes all the aims of life (SL 31); the gods obtained powers only by waiting at her gate (SL 93).

Contentment with limited attainments - the 'dream of ordinary knowledge' (Śiva Sūtra 2.4), the 'lower creation' in the middle stage (3.23), powers gained under the veil of delusion (3.6) - which falls short of liberation.
Pursuing indestructibility of the body and other powers as the goal; Allama's meeting with Gorakṣa shows the void body as higher.

name: Powers as a snare (riddhi-siddhi)
description: Yogic powers and feats, and attachment to inner lights and sounds for their own sake, which distract from the Lord.

name: Powers as obstacles
description: The powers arising from yoga are obstacles for one practising the highest yoga, a waste of time for one attaining the Lord; the devotee does not desire them.
antidotes: devotion that desires nothing but the Lord
concealment; living as if dull or deaf (DYŚ 93)
alt_description: The powers of the ghaṭa stage are obstacles to the great accomplishment; displaying them draws disciples and distracts from practice (DYŚ 91–94).
Powers arising from practice are obstacles to the great attainment; the yogin should hide them and not set his mind on them (Yogatattva 76–77; Varāha 3; Yogaśikhā 5.62).
Yogic powers distract the one seeking the Lord or the Self and waste time.

Tāyumāṉavar: every power, from taming beasts to transmuting metals and entering other bodies, is easier than stilling the mind — the powers are not the goal; Kuṭampai asks what need the knower has of kaṟpam and yoga.

name: Powers as obstacles in samādhi (upasarga)
description: Intuition and the divine senses, arising in the concentrated mind, are obstacles because they oppose seeing; they count as powers only in emergence (3.37, YBh 3.37).

name: Clinging to rules and observances
description: Taking rules and vows as themselves purifying (MN 2; Snp 4.9); the third fetter.

name: The three kinds of obstacle (Śiva Saṃhitā)
description: Obstacles to liberation in the form of enjoyment (learning, arts, wealth, family, sense-objects), of dharma (meditation-objects, mantra, gifts, fame, public works, sacrifices, vows, pilgrimages) and of knowledge (SS 5.2–8); many terrible obstacles, to be overcome by perseverance and the praṇava (3.47–48).
antidotes: repetition of the long praṇava in solitude (SS 3.48)

name: The six destroyers of yoga (HYP 1.15)
description: Overeating, overexertion, too much talk, clinging to rules, the company of people and unsteadiness destroy yoga.
antidotes: enthusiasm, boldness, patience, knowledge of truth, determination, renouncing company (HYP 1.16)

name: Six enemies (ṣaḍ-ripu)
description: Desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride and envy (Varāha 1).
alt_description: Desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride and envy, which the Bāul and Sahajiyā songs name as the enemies to be mastered before the Man can be held.

name: The six faults to be abandoned (Viduranīti)
description: Sleep, drowsiness, fear, anger, sloth and procrastination are to be abandoned by one who seeks prosperity (MBh 5.33.66).

name: The six hindrances of the Abhidhamma
description: Sensual desire, ill will, sloth-and-torpor, restlessness-and-remorse, doubt and ignorance.

equivalents.note: the sutta five plus ignorance

name: The six stains of defilement (kleśamala)
description: Deceit, dissimulation, pride, spite, enmity, harmfulness — secondary defilements traced to passion, aversion and view.

name: The six root afflictions (Yogācāra)
description: Greed, aversion, delusion, conceit, (wrong) views and doubt.

name: Six things that destroy devotion
description: Overeating or over-collecting, over-endeavour, idle talk, rigid attachment to (or neglect of) rules, worldly company, greed or fickleness.
antidotes: the six things that nourish devotion (Upadeśāmṛta 3)

name: Six waves (ūrmi)
description: Hunger, thirst, grief, delusion, old age and death (Varāha 1; Vajrasūci).

name: The sixteen defilements of the mind
description: Covetousness, ill will, anger, hostility, contempt, domineering, envy, avarice, deceit, fraud, obstinacy, presumption, conceit, arrogance, vanity, negligence (MN 7).

name: Grief (śoka)
description: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Arjuna's grief overwhelms him (1.47) and dries up his senses so that no kingdom could dispel it (2.8). Kṛṣṇa answers that the wise grieve neither for the dead nor the living (2.11) and repeatedly concludes 'you ought not to grieve' from the nature of the embodied self (2.25, 2.26, 2.27, 2.30).
antidotes: Knowledge that the embodied one is eternal and unslayable (2.11–30)
The certainty of death for the born (2.27)

alt_description: Nārada, knowing only mantras, is in sorrow; 'the knower of the self crosses sorrow' (ChU 7.1.3; MuU 3.2.9); for one who sees oneness there is no delusion or sorrow (Īśa 7); the wise leaves joy and sorrow (KU 1.2.12); seeing the Lord the grieving bird is freed from sorrow (MuU 3.1.2).

name: Vitiation of the channels
description: Excess flow, obstruction, knotting, or flow in the wrong path (Ca Vi 5.22), caused by the doṣas and by improper food and conduct.

name: Arrogance (stabdhatā)
description: Pride — especially the pride of thinking oneself Brahman — warned against in the gloss on 'tat tvam asi': 'in truth you are not that; let there be no arrogance in you'.

name: Clinging to the outer liṅga alone
description: Abandoning the inner liṅga of light and staying with outer liṅgas — called delusion at the prāṇaliṅgi stage.

name: Dullness (styāna)
description: The mind's unfitness for work. One of the nine obstacles (1.30, YBh 1.30).

name: The sun's swallowing of the moon's nectar (the cause of ageing)
description: The nectar that drips from the moon at the palate or crown is swallowed by the sun, the fire at the navel, and so the body grows old and falls under death's power; the throat lock, the inverted posture and khecarī are taught to prevent this.
notes: The doctrine behind it is U28's cpt:sun-moon-fire.

name: Taking emptiness as a view
description: Holding emptiness itself as a thesis or entity; the Victors called those who do so incurable, like a patient in whom the medicine itself stays unexpelled.
antidotes: cpt:emptiness-of-emptiness (understanding that emptiness too is empty)

name: Void, sleep-like absorption mistaken for the goal
description: A void state, like deep sleep, is artificial and not the principle (SK 1.12-13); in the great space where the breaths dissolve, the deluded yogin remains as in deep sleep while the awakened remains unveiled (SK 1.25); identification with the void is subordinate to consciousness (ĪPK 3.2.12-15).

name: Grasping at own-nature (inherent existence)
description: Taking things born of causes and conditions as existing by their own nature; the root of views, disputes and afflictions and, as ignorance, of the twelve links.

name: Natural afflictions: hunger, thirst, old age, death, sleep
description: The natural diseases — hunger, thirst, old age, death and sleep (Su Sū 1.25); diseases of old age and death arising from time's transformation have no remedy (Ca Śā 1.115).
antidotes: prc:rasayana (delays old age; does not abolish death in Āyurveda)

name: The conceit of independence (svātantrya)
description: Thinking oneself independent of the Lord, one's own master and one's own means — contrary to the soul's nature of dependence.

name: Fever (takman)
description: Recurrent fever, sent away to distant peoples by Atharvavedic charms.
notes: rests_on: tea:atharvaveda-saunaka:5.22

name: The marks of tamas and rajas (Maitrī 3.5)
description: MaiU 3.5 lists the marks of tamas (delusion, fear, despondency, sleep, sloth, heedlessness, old age, grief, hunger, thirst...) and of rajas (craving, affection, passion, greed, violence, lust, hatred, deceit...), with which the elemental self is filled.
antidotes: knowledge, austerity and one's own dharma (MaiU 4.3)
notes: List reconstructed from memory (low).

name: Tāmasa disposition
description: Hating all people, constantly making 'I', and holding untrue notions — removed by the guru at the tāmasanirasana sub-stage of the śaraṇa.

name: The four tāmasa dispositions
description: Non-virtue, non-knowledge, passion and powerlessness, the tāmasa form of buddhi (SK 23), leading respectively to downward movement, bondage, saṃsāra and obstruction (SK 44–45).
antidotes: virtue, knowledge, dispassion, power (the sāttvika dispositions)

name: Mixing of scriptural rules (tantra-saṅkara)
description: Performing a rite series by a different tantra from the one begun, or installing with a sub-division instead of a root scripture; the Kāmika says the latter destroys performer and patron.

name: The threefold suffering
description: Suffering from oneself (bodily and mental), from other beings, and from divine/natural powers; the spur to dispassion.

name: Obstacles in samādhi (Tejobindu)
description: Lack of inquiry, sloth, desire for enjoyment, dissolution (laya), darkness, distraction, radiance, sweating and blankness (Tejobindu 1.40–41).

name: Pollution of the temple (aśuddhi)
description: Events such as birth- or death-impurity, bloodshed or improper entry that pollute the sanctum and require purificatory rites before worship resumes.

name: The ten unwholesome courses of action
description: Killing, stealing, sexual misconduct; false, divisive, harsh speech and idle chatter; covetousness, ill will and wrong view (MN 41; AN 10.176).

name: The ten armies of Māra
description: Sensual desire, discontent, hunger and thirst, craving, sloth and torpor, fear, doubt, hypocrisy and obstinacy, gain and fame wrongly obtained, self-exaltation and contempt of others (Snp 3.2).

name: The ten fetters (saṃyojana)
description: Identity view, doubt, clinging to rules and vows, sensual lust and ill will (the five lower); lust for form, lust for the formless, conceit, restlessness and ignorance (the five higher) (MN 64).
alt_description: Lower: satkāya-view, attachment to rules and observances, doubt, sensual desire, malice — the first three the gate, the root and the grasping; higher: passion for form, for the formless, restlessness, pride, delusion.

equivalents.note: Two different fetter lists in the same text.

name: The ten fetters in the Abhidhamma list
description: The Abhidhamma's list of fetters, differing from the sutta list by including envy and avarice and counting lust for existence as one.

equivalents.note: the sutta list of ten fetters

name: The ten undefiled ignorances regarding the dharmadhātu
description: Ten non-afflicted ignorances concerning ten aspects of the dharmadhātu (its all-pervasiveness, supremacy etc.), whose antidotes are the ten grounds.
notes: Checked that MAV 2.16 names 'this undefiled tenfold ignorance regarding the dharmadhātu' with the grounds as antidotes; the list is in 2.14–15.

name: The ten defilements (kilesa-vatthu)
description: Greed, hatred, delusion, conceit, views, doubt, sloth, restlessness, shamelessness, fearlessness of wrongdoing.

equivalents.note: Yoga's five afflictions overlap (ignorance, I-am-ness/conceit, attachment, aversion, clinging to life)

name: The ten impediments (paḷibodha)
description: Things to be cut off before developing concentration; supernormal power is an impediment to insight, not to concentration.
antidotes: severing or settling each (e.g. medicine for affliction)

name: The ten imperfections of insight (vipassanūpakkilesa)
description: Experiences arising with tender insight into rise and fall that are mistaken for the path; grasped by view, conceit and craving they become thirty.
antidotes: discerning each as impermanent and 'not the path'

name: The thieving senses (kaḷḷap pulaṉ)
description: The five senses as thieves and a forest to be cut down and burnt before the 'house' of release can be seen (Kaṭuveḷi 13–14); cut off by the guru (Aḻukaṇṇi 34); burnt by the seeker (Pattirakiriyār 1); TM 1823 calls them the thieving senses that become the temple's lamps once tamed.

equivalents.note: the senses as obstacle

name: Dullness and drowsiness (thīnamiddha)
description: The third hindrance, fed by discontent, lethargy and sleepiness after meals (SN 46.51); remedies for drowsiness (AN 7.61).

name: The three unwholesome roots
description: Greed, hatred and delusion — the roots of the unwholesome (MN 9), the three fires (SN 35.28) and the sources of kamma (AN 3.34); their destruction is nibbāna (SN 38.1).

equivalents.note: the same three under the later name 'three poisons'
the Yoga kleśas include rāga and dveṣa; avidyā corresponds partly to moha

name: The three obstructions (āvaraṇa)
description: Obstruction of karma (the deadly acts), of defilement (intense defilement) and of ripening (bad destinies, birth in Kuru or among the non-perceiving gods), which prevent entering the path.

name: The three groups of faults (rāga, dveṣa, moha)
description: Faults are what impel to activity; they fall into three groups — attachment, aversion, delusion — delusion being the worst; they arise from false knowledge and from falsely constructed objects.
antidotes: knowledge of truth about their causes (NS 4.2.1)

equivalents.note: The Buddhist three roots/poisons (greed, hatred, delusion) have the same triad; Nyāya derives them from false knowledge about the self.

name: Three desires (eṣaṇā)
description: Desire for wife (sons), wealth and worlds, which the renouncer declares he has risen above (Nāradaparivrājaka 4.38; after Bṛhadāraṇyaka 3.5.1).
alt_description: Kaṭuveḷi: 'the three desires are evil' (5); in the Siddha list of ninety-six they are the desires for wife, children and wealth (list recalled at low confidence).

name: The three gates of hell: desire, anger, greed
description: Desire, anger and greed are the threefold gate of hell, destructive of the self, to be abandoned (BhG 16.21–22).

name: The three impurities (mala-traya)
description: In the Pratyabhijñā: the āṇava impurity (loss of freedom by awareness, or awareness without freedom), the māyīya (appearance of the knowable as separate) and the kārma (agency in an unconscious agent); all three arise through the power of māyā (ĪPK 3.2.4-5). The root impurity is ignorance, not a substance (TĀ 1.22-23, MVT 1.23).

equivalents.note: Śaiva Siddhānta's three bonds share names but the Siddhānta holds āṇava to be a real substance removable only by ritual action

alt_description: Āṇava, karma and māyā — eternal bonds that cover the soul's powers; removed (Sanskrit) or rendered powerless (Tamil) by Śiva's grace.
Āṇava, māyīya and kārma impurity binding the soul, from which Śiva is free and which are shaken off at union.
Counted among the ninety-six principles (malam 3); Paṭṭiṉattār speaks of fleeing 'the woman called māyā-mala' to the mother, grace (Tiruvēkampamālai 10).

name: The three follies (mūḍhatā)
description: Folly regarding the world (bathing in rivers, heaping stones for merit), regarding gods (worshipping passionate deities for favours) and regarding false ascetics — faults of right view (Ratnakaraṇḍa).

name: The three roots of bad (greed, hatred, delusion)
description: In the desire realm passion, aversion and delusion are the three bad roots (AK 5.20); the contemplation of the unlovely counters passion.

name: The three thorns (śalya)
description: Deceit, longing for future reward and wrong view, which disqualify a vow-holder (TS 7.18).

name: Three vāsanās (for the world, scripture and body)
description: Vāsanās for social esteem, for scriptural learning and for the body, which prevent true knowledge (Muktikā 2).
alt_description: Tendencies toward the world (reputation), toward scriptural learning (pedantry) and toward the body, which prevent right knowledge — 'iron fetters'.

name: The three bonds (prakṛti-, vaikārika-, dakṣiṇā-bandha)
description: Bondage to prakṛti (absorption from taking the eight prakṛtis as highest), to the modifications (renunciants and worldly people ruled by senses and objects) and through gifts (given with conceit by students, householders, mendicants and forest-dwellers).

name: Concealment (tirobhāva) as the Lord's binding power
description: The first of Śrī's five acts, by which the soul's true nature is concealed; ended by grace.

equivalents.note: the Śaiva concealing power (U18/U19)

name: The threefold bond
description: The self's bondage to the world as body (seat of experience), senses (instruments) and objects (what is experienced).
antidotes: exhaustion of dharma and adharma (see pth:kumarila-moksa)

name: Craving (tṛṣṇā)
description: Thirst, from which with attachment rajas arises and binds by attachment to action (BhG 14.7).
alt_description: Craving that grows with fulfilment; condemned by Rāma in the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha's first book and sung against in the Maṅki and Kāma Gītās.

name: The turbulent senses (indriyāṇi pramāthīni)
description: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The turbulent senses forcibly carry off the mind even of a discerning person who strives (2.60); the mind that follows the roving senses carries off wisdom as the wind a ship (2.67).
alt_description: The senses are turbulent and carry off the mind even of a striving wise man, as the wind carries off a ship (BhG 2.60, 2.67); attraction and aversion lurk in each sense (3.34).

name: Contentment (tuṣṭi): the nine complacencies
description: Nine false contentments (SK 50): resting content with knowing prakṛti; with outward means such as the triple staff and water-pot; with the thought that time will bring liberation; with luck; and five from abstaining from objects for seeing their faults — none brings liberation, lacking knowledge of the principles; with error and incapacity they curb accomplishment (SK 51).

name: The twenty-one kinds of pain
description: What is to be abandoned: pain in twenty-one kinds (body, six senses, six objects, six cognitions, pleasure and pain), whose absolute cessation is liberation.
notes: The number is confirmed; the member list is from later manuals (recalled).

name: The twenty secondary afflictions
description: Anger, enmity, concealment, spite, envy, avarice, deceit, dishonesty, pride, harmfulness, shamelessness, non-embarrassment, torpor, agitation, lack of faith, laziness, heedlessness, forgetfulness, distraction and non-awareness.

name: The twenty-two hardships
description: Hunger, thirst, cold, heat and the other afflictions that may make an ascetic swerve from the path unless endured (TS 9.8–9).

name: The obscurations of afflictions and of the knowable
description: The obscuration of afflictions (kleśāvaraṇa), which prevents liberation, and the obscuration of the knowable (jñeyāvaraṇa), which prevents omniscience; emptiness is the antidote to both.
alt_description: Yogācāra contribution: all obscurations are summed up as the afflictive obscuration (removed by the selflessness of persons) and the cognitive obscuration (removed by the selflessness of dharmas); liberation follows their exhaustion.

name: The view of annihilation (uccheda-diṭṭhi)
description: The extreme that the being is annihilated at death; with eternalism one of the two extremes.

name: Restlessness (fetter)
description: The ninth fetter.

name: Restlessness and remorse (uddhaccakukkucca)
description: The fourth hindrance, fed by unsettledness of mind (SN 46.51).

name: The three obstacles to service (Sevāphala)
description: Agitation of mind (udvega), external hindrance (pratibandha) and attachment to enjoyment (bhoga), which impede the fruits of service.

name: Giving or receiving the teaching without testing
description: Guru and disciple who give and receive without testing each other both become piśācas; knowledge does not stay in the unworthy (Kulārṇava 14.11-14; 2.36).

name: Grasping (upadhā) and craving
description: Upadhā is the supreme cause of suffering and its seats; craving taken up from objects binds the ignorant like the silkworm's threads; renouncing all upadhā ends all suffering (Ca Śā 1.94-97, 1.134-135).

equivalents.note: Buddhist craving as the origin of suffering

alt_description: A fault of disposition by which the practices of the life-stages fail to yield merit; its absence (anupadhā) is purity of intention.

name: Bondage by real adjuncts (Bhāskara)
description: The soul's delimitation by real adjuncts (body, senses, intellect) due to beginningless karma and ignorance; they end only with the body.

name: Secondary sins (upapātaka)
description: A long list of lesser offences — killing a cow, neglecting the fires or the Veda, selling oneself, usury, deserting parents or teacher, adultery, killing women, śūdras, vaiśyas or kṣatriyas, unbelief (nāstikya) and others (MDh 11.59–66).

name: The six upasargas (Liṅga/Śiva Purāṇa)
description: Pratibhā, śravaṇa, vārtā, darśana, āsvāda and vedanā - powers of knowing, hearing, speech-understanding, seeing, tasting and touching the divine - which in the state of emergence are obstacles and are to be renounced by supreme dispassion.

name: The upasargas of the Mārkaṇḍeya
description: After the self is seen: longings for ritual rewards, women, heaven, divinity, elixirs and supernatural feats; then five states - prātibha, śrāvaṇa, daiva, bhrama, āvarta - by which even the gods lose their yoga and return.
antidotes: the mental white blanket and contemplation of Brahman (MkP 40.14-15)

name: Offences after surrender or knowledge (uttarāgha)
description: Sins committed after the attainment of knowledge or surrender: unintentional ones do not cling; deliberate ones require expiation or renewed surrender (Vaṭakalai) or are corrected by the Lord (Teṅkalai).

name: Disputation (vāda)
description: Argument is not to be resorted to, because it gives room for excess and is inconclusive (NBS 74–75).

name: The impurities of speech (vāṅ-mala, apaśabda)
description: Incorrect and corrupt word-forms and faulty pronunciation, which grammar 'heals' (VP 1.14); the Asuras were defeated for mispronunciation, and a mantra wrong in tone or letter harms the sacrificer.

name: Confusion of the classes (varṇasaṅkara)
description: As the tradition states it: the mixing of classes through unions and abandonment of one's own dharma, which the texts regard as destroying the social order (Arthaśāstra 1.3.15; MDh 10).
notes: Recorded faithfully; critiques belong to other units.

local Manu 10.24, 10.61

Recorded as the tradition states it.

name: The fetters of Varuṇa (pāśa)
description: The upper, middle and lower fetters with which Varuṇa binds the offender; loosened by his grace so that one becomes sinless before Aditi.
notes: rests_on: tea:rgveda:1.24.15, tea:rgveda:7.88.7, tea:atharvaveda-saunaka:4.16.2-6

name: Aggravation of vāta
description: Vāta increases by the repeated use of dry, light, cold, rough and clear things, exertion, fasting, waking, grief and the like, especially in the rains, at dawn and afternoon and after digestion; increased, it brings roughness of voice, emaciation, darkness, tremor, desire for warmth, sleeplessness, weakness and hard stools; provoked, it afflicts body and mind, causing fear, grief, delusion and confusion.

name: Suppression of the natural urges
description: Holding back or forcing the natural urges is the cause of many diseases (Ca Sū 7.3-25; AHS Sū 4).

name: Outward show without devotion
description: Wearing the marks of a devotee or performing worship for show while the heart is elsewhere — the target of Ambigara Cauḍayya's and Basava's criticism.

name: Doubt (vicikicchā)
description: The fifth hindrance and second fetter: doubt about the teacher, the teaching and the training; abandoned at stream-entry (MN 2).

name: Lapse or defect in ritual (vidhilopa, chidra)
description: Omissions and errors in the prescribed rites, which the annual pavitra offering and expiatory rites make good.

name: Pride of learning
description: The proud who ponder many books go to a bad end; knowledge is not had by millions of books (Akulavīra B.76–78).

name: The view of emptiness (śūnyatādṛṣṭi)
description: Taking emptiness itself as a view or as annihilation — 'incurable', worse than a view of self as large as Sumeru; the RGV criticizes those 'distracted about emptiness'.

name: Obstructors of ritual (vighna)
description: Beings and forces that obstruct worship; at the start of rites they are driven away with the weapon-mantra (astra) and Gaṇeśa/Vighneśvara is worshipped.

name: Thought-constructs (vikalpa) as bondage
description: Dichotomizing thought, permeated by words, veils one's nature and is the form of the 'personal' ignorance (Tantrasāra 1; SK 3.14-15); dream is vikalpa (Śiva Sūtra 1.9).
antidotes: the thought-free dhāraṇās of the Vijñāna Bhairava

name: Distraction (vikṣepa)
description: The mind's running to external things; it should be calmed again (GK 3.44).
alt_description: Sāṃkhya contribution: distraction in meditation, to be turned away from (SS 6.30).

Yogācāra contribution: the mind straying from its object, to be noticed quickly and brought back (MSA 14.11); the Madhyāntavibhāga lists kinds of distraction (emerging, toward objects, relishing sinking and agitation, expectation, (hidden) intention, self-conceit in attention, lower mind).
The mind's wandering to worldly topics during practice.
notes: The Madhyāntavibhāga list is paraphrased from 5.12–13 (checked in the e-text) without the bhāṣya's glosses.
alt_notes: Partial parallel: Vedāntasāra's vikṣepa (list of obstacles to nirvikalpa samādhi; U13). Viśvanātha adds apratipatti.

name: The five accompaniments of distraction
description: Pain (threefold), dejection, trembling of the limbs, and [disturbed] inhalation and exhalation accompany the distractions; they occur in the distracted, not the concentrated, mind (1.31, YBh 1.31).

name: Contrary habitual notion (viparīta-bhāvanā)
description: The deep-rooted habit of taking oneself to be body and mind, persisting after understanding; removed by contemplation.

name: Error (viparyaya): the five-jointed avidyā
description: Five kinds of error with sixty-two subdivisions (SK 47–48): darkness (8), delusion (8), great delusion (10), gloom (18), blind gloom (18) — taking the eight prakṛtis for the self and thinking oneself liberated, attachment to the eight powers, attachment to the ten objects, resentment over powers and objects, and despair at losing them in death.

equivalents.note: identified with avidyā, asmitā, rāga, dveṣa, abhiniveśa by the Yoga Bhāṣya on YS 1.8

name: Incompatible food (viruddha āhāra)
description: Foods that conflict with the body's tissues by opposed qualities, combination, preparation, place, time, dose or nature — e.g. fish with milk — vitiating the blood and sometimes fatal (Ca Sū 26.81-92).

name: Poison and venom performance
description: Religious acts done for this-worldly gain ('poison') or heavenly reward ('venom'), and mechanical performance, which do not lead to liberation (Yogabindu).

name: Despondency (viṣāda)
description: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Arjuna, overcome by pity and despairing on seeing his kin, describes his limbs failing, mouth drying, trembling, hair standing on end, the bow slipping, skin burning, inability to stand and a whirling mind (1.28–30; also 2.1, 2.10).
antidotes: the teacher's instruction on the self and on svadharma (2.11–38)
alt_description: Arjuna's grief and dejection on seeing his kinsmen — trembling, dry mouth, failing limbs, confusion about dharma, faint-heartedness (kārpaṇya) — which moves him to lay down his bow (BhG 1.28–47; 2.1–7).

name: Viṣṭi (Bhadrā) karaṇa
description: The inauspicious half-lunar-day Viṣṭi, unfit for undertakings; births under it need pacification (BPHS 88).

name: Harmful thoughts (vitarka): violence and the rest
description: Thoughts of violence, untruth, stealing, incontinence and possessiveness, done, caused or approved, from greed, anger or delusion, mild to intense; their fruit is endless suffering and ignorance (2.33–34, YBh 2.33–34).

name: Transgressions of the vows
description: Five partial lapses for each vow and virtue (TS 7.24–37), e.g. binding, beating, mutilating, overloading and starving for non-violence.

name: Illness (vyādhi)
description: Imbalance of the bodily elements, fluids and organs. One of the nine obstacles (1.30, YBh 1.30).

name: Delusion by one's own powers
description: Not knowing that one performs the five acts, one is deluded by one's own powers - this is transmigration (PH 12); the powers arising from the mass of sounds veil one's nature, since no idea arises without words (SK 3.13-16).
antidotes: recognition of the powers as one's own (PH 13)

name: The eighteen vices of a king
description: Ten born of desire (hunting, gambling, day-sleep, censoriousness, women, drink, singing, music, dancing, idle roaming) and eight born of anger (slander, violence, treachery, envy, calumny, seizure of property, abuse, assault) (MDh 7.45–48).

name: Impressions of emergence (vyutthāna-saṃskāra)
description: Impressions of the outgoing mind that compete with those of stilling (3.9) and overpower them when the latter are weak (YBh 3.10); the impression born of samādhi-insight obstructs them (YBh 1.50).

name: Attachment to worldly supernormal powers
description: The fragile powers of a worldling distract from insight and are easily lost.
antidotes: severing the impediment of powers before insight

equivalents.note: YS 3.37's warning that the powers are obstacles to samādhi

name: Talk of lust, wealth, unbelievers and enemies
description: Stories of women (as objects of lust), wealth, unbelievers and enemies are not to be listened to (NBS 63).

name: Consumption, wasting disease (yakṣma)
description: Wasting disease and disease in general, with jaundice and heart-disease, driven out by hymns, plants and amulets.
notes: rests_on: tea:atharvaveda-saunaka:3.7, tea:atharvaveda-saunaka:1.22

name: 'I' and 'mine' (yāṉ, eṉatu)
description: The pride of self and possession, whose destruction leads beyond the gods' world (Kuṟaḷ 346).

equivalents.note: ego-sense and possessiveness

name: Faults from practising yoga at the wrong time or place
description: Practising overfed, hungry, tired or agitated, in extreme cold, heat or wind, or in noisy, fiery, dangerous and impure places brings deafness, dullness, loss of memory, dumbness, blindness and fever; remedies are prescribed.
antidotes: care of the body as the means of the four aims
a hidden hut in a good land; beginning in spring or autumn (GS 5.5–9)
alt_description: Beginning yoga in a distant land (no trust), forest (no food), capital or crowd (exposure), or in winter, summer or the rains brings failure or disease (GS 5.3–9).

name: Ten obstacles (Yogakuṇḍalī)
description: Disease, doubt, heedlessness, sloth, sleep, withdrawal of interest, delusion and further obstacles (readings uncertain), ending in failure to attain the truth of yoga; disease arises from wrong conduct such as day-sleep and excess.

name: The twenty faults of the jīva (Yogatattva)
description: Twenty faults that bind the jīva; free of them it is called Śiva (Yogatattva 12–13; Yogaśikhā 1.10–11).

name: Obstacles at the start of practice (Yogatattva)
description: Sloth, boasting, the company of rogues, pursuit of mantras and the like, and craving for metals and women — mirages to be abandoned (Yogatattva 30–31).

name: Sexual association, as the renunciant texts frame it (strī-saṅga)
description: Texts addressed to male renunciants warn that attachment to women and to men attached to women binds more than any other (the moth, the elephant, Purūravas); the Kapila Gītā applies the parallel warning to a woman's attachment to husband, children and home; the Avadhūta Gītā's eighth chapter states it in harsh terms. Recorded as the texts state it.
